strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical privacy-utility tradeoff in LLM services
Rigorous dataset construction with comprehensive human verification (95.1% inter-annotator agreement)
Systematic evaluation across multiple model scales and prompting strategies with clear findings about model limitations
Thoughtfully designed specialized test sets (PII-hard, PII-distract) targeting challenging scenarios
Clear formal task definition with three well-structured evaluation tasks
Comprehensive appendices with detailed prompts, generation methodology, and annotation guidelines
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—primarily a resource paper without new algorithms or models; the 'query-unrelated masking strategy' is intuitive but not algorithmically novel
All-synthetic dataset with unknown generalization to real-world PII patterns and specialized domains (medical, financial)
Incomplete evaluation of primary task—query-unrelated masking results lack direct validation that masked text preserves LLM functionality or maintains semantic coherence
Query relevance formulation may be oversimplified as binary classification; borderline/contextual relevance cases not addressed
Minimal error analysis—paper reports performance numbers but provides little investigation into failure patterns or why models struggle with query-relevance reasoning
Missing statistical rigor—no significance tests, confidence intervals for model results, or error bars; cannot assess if performance differences are meaningful
No comparison with existing anonymization/de-identification systems or privacy protection baselines beyond 'mask all PII'
Dataset composition bias—all annotators from top universities in China with potential geographic/cultural bias in PII definitions and distributions
Prompting strategy analysis shows marginal and inconsistent improvements but lacks theoretical explanation of why certain strategies fail
Insufficient analysis of human-model performance gaps—human baseline provided but not analyzed for strategies employed or error patterns

strengths: Addresses a relevant and timely problem: query-aware privacy protection in LLM systems
Comprehensive benchmark with 2,842 carefully annotated samples across 55 fine-grained PII categories
Well-documented evaluation framework with detailed prompts, metrics, and annotation guidelines
Systematic evaluation across multiple model scales and prompting strategies provides useful empirical baselines
Clear motivation and problem formulation with helpful motivation figure (Figure 1)
Extensive human verification with 25 trained annotators and inter-annotator agreement metrics
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: proposes no novel methods, only a problem formulation; all baselines use existing approaches (BiLSTM-CRF, standard LLM prompting)
Entirely synthetic data without real-world validation; no comparison with existing privacy benchmarks (e.g., TAB) or evaluation on actual user prompts

Inadequate privacy analysis: lacks formal privacy definitions (differential privacy, k-anonymity), never validates that query-unrelated PII is actually less sensitive, no adversarial evaluation of masking effectiveness
Shallow experimental insights: documents poor model performance but provides minimal analysis of why; no error analysis, no explanation of which query/PII types cause failures, no ablation studies

Severe practical limitation: best-performing approach (Naive w/ Choice, F1=0.82) requires candidate entities, which paper admits are rarely available in real scenarios, undermining deployment viability
Narrow human evaluation: only 25 annotators from same region; 91.5% inter-annotator agreement suggests ambiguity in task definition but is not thoroughly analyzed
Missing comparisons: no direct evaluation on existing benchmarks or comparison with prior work (Papadopoulou et al. 2022); unclear what is genuinely new

Synthetic data generation concerns: heavy GPT-4 dependence, arbitrary consistency rules, manually balanced PII distribution may not reflect real-world scenarios; no validation of realistic task difficulty

Incomplete analysis: large Strict-F1 vs. Ent-F1 gaps unexplained; performance degradation beyond 5 subjects not investigated; inconsistent prompting effects (Self-Consistency helps sometimes, hurts others) without principled explanation
Task definition redundancy: three proposed tasks but Task 3 (masking) appears to be just Tasks 1+2 combined, not a fundamentally new contribution
No statistical rigor: missing significance tests, confidence intervals, and error bars in most results

Questionable privacy assumptions: assumes query-unrelated PII masking provides privacy but never validates against reconstruction attacks or discusses inference risks; type-tag masking may still leak information

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical importance: query-aware privacy protection balances utility and security in a nuanced way
Rigorous dataset construction with thoughtful multi-stage synthesis, 2,842 samples, 55 PII categories, and validation by 25 domain experts with high inter-annotator agreement (95.1%/91.5%)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across model classes (traditional, SLM, open-source LLM, API LLM), prompting strategies, and multiple metrics revealing interpretable findings
Clear, important findings: strong PII detection (>90% F1) masks critical weakness in query relevance determination (F1 <0.63), with dramatic degradation in realistic complexity scenarios
Detailed methodology, transparent reporting, and explicit discussion of ethical considerations regarding data privacy and bias mitigation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the 'query-unrelated PII masking strategy' is problem formulation rather than method innovation; actual masking mechanisms are not proposed
Exclusive reliance on synthetic data (GPT-4 generated) without validation on real-world data where PII usage patterns may differ substantially, limiting generalization claims
Incomplete evaluation of the masking system: no formal assessment of masked text quality, coherence, semantic utility preservation, or end-to-end downstream task performance
Insufficient analysis of why models fail: reasoning processes not captured, minimal qualitative error analysis, and no systematic failure mode investigation despite acknowledged limitations

Query relevance annotation lacks clear definition of 'necessary for answering'—appears subjective with lower inter-annotator agreement (91.5%) suggesting inherent ambiguity; resolution strategies not detailed

Evaluation primarily assesses detection rather than masking effectiveness; Task 3 depends entirely on Tasks 1-2 outcomes without independent validation of whether identified PII suffices for query answering
Limited demonstration of practical utility: no evidence that benchmark-driven improvements actually enhance system performance on real privacy-utility tradeoffs
Restricted to English with no cross-lingual evaluation; specialized domain coverage (medical, financial) acknowledged as missing but dismissed; narrow scope despite breadth claims

strengths: Well-motivated and practically important problem: The query-aware privacy protection task clearly articulates tension between utility and privacy, with effective motivation in Figure 1.

Comprehensive dataset construction: 2,842 carefully designed samples across 7 PII types with 55 subcategories; multiple dataset variants; rigorous human verification with high inter-annotator agreement (κ=0.912 for PII detection).
Novel task formulation: The three-tier evaluation framework (PII Detection → Query-Related Detection → Query-Unrelated Masking) clearly distinguishes between identification and relevance assessment.
Rigorous evaluation methodology: Multiple baseline models and prompting strategies; privacy-utility tradeoff analysis; strong validation (Spearman ρ>0.988) between synthetic and real-world data.
Thorough documentation: Clear presentation, detailed appendices, comprehensive annotation guidelines, and well-designed annotation platform.
Practical relevance: Addresses real privacy risks in LLM deployments where users submit prompts containing sensitive information.
weaknesses: Limited technical and methodological novelty: Primarily a dataset/benchmark paper without proposing new models, algorithms, or learning approaches. The query-unrelated masking strategy is conceptually straightforward.

Insufficient diagnostic analysis: While showing poor performance (0.627 F1), the paper lacks error analysis, failure case taxonomy, or investigation into why models fail at relevance assessment. Acknowledged but unaddressed limitation in Section Limitations.

Query relevance assessment quality concerns: Lower inter-annotator agreement for query-related detection (κ=0.873 vs 0.912) without analysis of disagreement patterns. Subjectivity of relevance (multi-hop, implicit relevance) not adequately addressed.

Dataset bias from reliance on GPT-4: Both data generation and consistency checking use GPT-4, potentially encoding its reasoning patterns. This could bias the benchmark toward GPT-4-favorable patterns.
Limited real-world validation: Only 100 samples from 20 AI researchers (narrow demographic). Insufficient to validate coverage across diverse scenarios, languages, domains, and cultural contexts.
Large performance-to-practice gap: Even advanced models achieve ~0.72 F1 vs. 0.95 human performance. No proposed solutions, no user studies on acceptance, no threshold analysis for deployment.

Missing comparative analysis: No comparison with existing privacy-preserving systems beyond basic masking; no comparison with related work (differential privacy, federated learning, IR relevance); limited discussion of privacy regulation compliance.
Incomplete error analysis: Figure 4 shows performance degrades sharply with complexity (5+ subjects: F1 drops from 0.85 to 0.52) but provides no investigation of root causes or mitigation strategies.
Evaluation metric concerns: RougeL-F fuzzy matching may be too lenient for PII entities; arbitrary weighting in Balanced Score (0.5/0.5) without domain-specific justification.

Missing practical considerations: No user studies on privacy-utility acceptance; no analysis of deployment costs/latency; no investigation of streaming scenarios; no adversarial robustness analysis; no fairness evaluation across demographic groups.

strengths: Well-motivated privacy problem with careful, multi-stage dataset construction including consistency optimization and human verification with strong inter-annotator agreement (κ=0.912)
Comprehensive benchmark covering diverse scenarios (single/multi-subject, 7 PII types with 55 subcategories, 2,842 samples) with specialized challenging test sets
Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple model families (traditional NER, API LLMs, open-source LLMs, SLMs) and prompting strategies (6+ approaches tested)
Practical privacy-utility tradeoff analysis demonstrating concrete effectiveness (P=0.83, U=0.89) of proposed masking strategy
Solid methodology with clear task definitions, multiple evaluation metrics, and validation attempt via PII-Real dataset
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: The 'query-unrelated PII masking strategy' is intuitive but not a novel methodological contribution—it builds directly on existing work (Papadopoulou et al. 2022, Shen et al. 2024) without algorithmic innovation. The paper is primarily a benchmark rather than introducing new techniques

Weak real-world validation undermines central claims: 95% of dataset is synthetically generated by GPT-4; PII-Real validation set contains only 100 samples from 20 researchers; high synthetic-real consistency scores (0.98+) could indicate oversimplified data rather than genuine alignment

Inadequate failure analysis: No error categorization, case studies, or investigation of why models fail; massive unexplained performance gap between Naive (0.627 F1) and Naive w/ Choice (0.842 F1) suggests task may test selection ability rather than understanding, but this is not investigated

Task formulation concerns: The core challenges (PII detection, relevance assessment, selective masking) are straightforward applications of existing NLP techniques; no evidence that novel methods are required; unclear what specific technical innovations the benchmark demands

Unclear practical applicability: Paper focuses on classification tasks rather than building actual privacy protection systems; provides no concrete guidance for practitioners integrating this into real LLM applications; claims about 'substantial room for improvement' lack actionable direction

Dataset representativeness limitations: Single language (English only); synthetic prompts lack naturalism of real user interactions; limited domain diversity (healthcare, finance, legal mentioned as gaps but not addressed); human baseline from limited demographic pool (25 graduate students from 'top universities'); high human performance (95%+ F1) suggests task may be simpler than framed

Insufficient methodological rigor: Human evaluation on only 14% of samples (400/2,842); no statistical significance testing between models; missing ablation studies on dataset construction choices; arbitrary α=0.5 in balanced score; no inter-model comparison confidence intervals

Limited novelty in related work positioning: Insufficient differentiation from existing benchmarks (TAB, LLM-PBE); no comparison of different selective masking approaches; unclear how query-aware assessment differs fundamentally from standard relevance judgment

strengths: Comprehensive, rigorously constructed benchmark dataset with 2,842 samples across 7 PII types and 55 subcategories, featuring systematic synthesis with consistency optimization and high inter-annotator agreement (κ=0.912)

Thorough experimental evaluation across multiple model classes (traditional, API-based LLMs, open-source LLMs, SLMs) and prompting strategies with clear, actionable findings about model performance gaps

Timely and practically important problem addressing the privacy-utility tradeoff with intuitive problem formulation (query-unrelated PII masking); real-world validation with PII-Real dataset shows high consistency (ρ>0.988)
Excellent reproducibility and presentation with detailed task definitions, comprehensive appendices, implementation details, and annotation guidelines enabling future research

Clear empirical insights demonstrating models excel at PII detection (F1~0.89-0.90) but struggle with query relevance (F1~0.63-0.72), with performance degrading sharply in complex scenarios (5+ subjects)
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: contribution is primarily benchmarking rather than novel methods; 'query-unrelated PII masking' is a problem formulation not a technical innovation; no approaches proposed to address identified limitations

Incomplete privacy validation using only literal entity presence without adversarial evaluation or formal privacy guarantees; privacy score (Eq. 17) is binary and doesn't capture sophisticated inference attacks or partial leakage

Narrow utility evaluation using simple metrics (semantic similarity, LLM-as-Judge with Claude 3.5-Sonnet); missing evaluation of actual downstream task performance degradation; no user studies validating practical utility

Limited real-world validation: PII-Real comprises only 100 instances from 20 AI researchers in same professional domain; synthetic data may not capture full diversity of real-world PII distributions; domain-specific coverage not demonstrated

Insufficient analysis of failure modes: Figure 4 shows degradation but limited investigation of why; no systematic error categorization; missing analysis of which PII types or query structures cause greatest difficulty

Experimental design gaps: human baseline from only 25 annotators; 'Naive w/ Choice' condition unrealistic; no statistical significance testing between prompting strategies; consistency optimization uses specific LLM (GPT-4-0806) potentially introducing bias

Practical deployment gaps: no computational cost analysis; missing guidelines for practitioners on strategy selection; no guidance on handling uncertainty or confidence thresholds; unclear how to operationalize in production systems

Dataset scope limitations: primarily English-centric professional contexts; specialized domains (medical, financial) acknowledged but not addressed; unclear generalization to non-English languages or domains; claim of flexible expansion undemonstrated
